questions.qtext: Which of the following represents the value of $\displaystyle{}\int_1^e \frac{\ln (x)}{x} d x ?$
questions.solution:
Answer: C

Source solution 1 (score: 8)

Detailed Video Solution: https://youtu.be/6aIuj2b2J38

We note that $\dfrac{d}{d x}(\ln (x))=\dfrac{1}{x}$. So we perform the substitution $u=\ln (x)$. We see that $d u=\frac{1}{x} d x$. It follows that
$$
\int_1^e \frac{\ln (x)}{x} d x=\int_0^1 u d u=\left.\frac{1}{2} u^2\right|_0 ^1=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Source solution 2 (score: 0)
By substitution method choose $u=lnx$

so $\frac{du}{dx} = \frac{1}{x}$ $\rightarrow$ $du = \frac{1}{x}dx$ , the next step is to change the upper and lower limit.

then it will be, $\int_{0}^1 u du $ = $\left[\frac{u^2}{2}\right]_{0}^1$

=$\left[\frac{1}{2}-\frac{0}{2}\right]$

=$\frac{1}{2}$

option C is correct one.

$\int x.e^{-3x} \, dx$

options.text: If $\displaystyle{}\lim _{x \rightarrow 5} f(x)=0$ and $\displaystyle{}\lim _{x \rightarrow 5} g(x)=0$, then $\displaystyle{}\lim _{x \rightarrow 5} \frac{f(x)}{g(x)}$ does not exist.
If $f, g,$ are any two functions which are continuous for all $x$, then $\dfrac{f}{g}$ is continuous for all $x$.
It is possible that functions $f$ and $g$ are not continuous at a point $x_0,$ but $f+g$ is continuous at $x_0$.
If $f^{\prime}(c)=0$ then $f(x)$ has a local maximum or a local minimum at $x=c$.

questions.solution:
Answer: C

Source solution 1 (score: 9)

Detailed Video Solution: https://youtu.be/6aIuj2b2J38

Option B -
If $f, g,$ are any two functions which are continuous for all $x$, then $\frac{f}{g}$ is continuous for all $x$.
False, Take $g(x)=0$.

Option C-
It is possible that functions $f$ and $g$ are not continuous at a point $x_0$, but $f+g$ is continuous at $x_0$.
True, take
$$
f(x)= \begin{cases}\dfrac{1}{x} & \text { if } x \neq 0 \\ \\ 0 & \text { if } x=0\end{cases}
$$
and $g(x)=-f(x).$

Source solution 2 (score: 8)
A) Consider $f(x) = (x-5)^2$ and $g(x)=(x-5)$ both functions approaches to 0 as x approaches to 5,

when it comes to $\lim_{x\to5}\dfrac{f(x)}{g(x)}$ = $\lim_{x\to5}(x-5)$ = 0, so option A is incorrect.

B) consider $f(x) = \sin x$ and $\text{g(x)}=\mathrm{x}$, both of these are continuous for all real $x$, but $\dfrac{f}{g}$ is not continuous at $x=0$, moreover its removable discontinuity which means you can redefine $\dfrac{f}{g}$ at $x=0$ which makes the function continuous at $x=0$.(you can verify it.). So option B is incorrect.



C) Consider

$f(x) = \begin{cases} 1 ,& \mathrm{x} \geq 0\\ -1, & \mathrm{x} < 0\end{cases}$

$g(x) = \begin{cases} -1 ,& \mathrm{x} \geq 0\\ 1, & \mathrm{x} < 0\end{cases}$

$(f + g)(x) = \begin{cases} 0 ,& \mathrm{x} \geq 0\\ 0, & \mathrm{x} < 0\end{cases} $

Both $f(x)$ , and $g(x)$ are discontinuous at $x=0$, but their sum is just a constant function that is continuous everywhere.
so it's possible to have a sum of two functions continuous at $x=a$, but when we consider each of them individually they will be discontinuous at $x=a$. so option C is correct.


D) Consider $f(x) = x^3$, it's s derivative is $0$ at $x=0$ but at $x=0$ its nether a local max or min. So option D is incorrect.

questions.qtext: Suppose $f(x)$ is continuous and diffrentiable for all $x$. And $-1 \leq f^{\prime}(x) \leq 3$ fo all $x$. Which of the following is/are ALWAYS true?
questions.solution:
Answer: A, B, C, D

Source solution 1 (score: 9)

$-1 \leq f'(x) \leq 3.$

Integrating all sides wrt. to $x$,

$\cancel{-x + c_1 \leq f(x) + c_2 \leq 3x + c_3 \qquad (1)}$

From eq $(1)$ we see that,

$\begin{align*}
\cancel{f(5) + c_2 \leq 15 + c_3 \qquad (2)} \\
\cancel{f(3) + c_2 \leq 9 + c_3 \qquad (3)}
\end{align*}
$

$\cancel{(2) – (3)}$

$\cancel{f(5) – f(3) \leq 6 \implies f(5) \leq f(3) + 6 \leq f(3) + 10}$

$\underline{Mistake}\text{: Inequality doesn't hold when both sides are subtracted by different values.}$

[Source: Lakshmi Narayana's comment below]

Correct approach:

$-1 \leq f'(x) \leq 3.$

Integrating all sides wrt. to $x$ from $3\ to\ 5$,

$\begin{align*}
- \int_{3}^{5} \,dx\ &\leq \int_{3}^{5} f'(x) \,dx\ \leq \int_{3}^{5} 3 \,dx
\qquad {\large [}\ \because \text{If } f(x) \leq g(x) \text{ for all } x \in [a,b] \text{ then } \int_a^b f(x)dx\leq \int_a^b g(x)dx\ {\large ]} \\ \\
-2\ &\leq f(5) - f(3)\ \leq 6 \qquad \to \text{(1)} \\
\end{align*}$

From eq. $(1)$ we see that,

$f(5) - f(3) \leq 6 \implies f(5) \leq f(3) + 6 \leq f(3) + 10$

$\therefore$ options $\textbf{ A. & C.}$ are correct.

Also from eq. $(1)$,

$f(5) - f(3) \geq -2 \implies f(5) \geq f(3) - 2 \geq f(3) - 10$

$\therefore$ options $\textbf{ B. & D.}$ are correct

Source solution 2 (score: 6)

Ans: A,B,C,D

Source solution 3 (score: 5)

Given that f(x) is differentiable and continuous for all x. And f’(x) $\in$ [-1,3] for all x.

So, $\exists$y $\in$(3,5) suct that f’(y) = [f(5) – f(3)] / [5 – 3] = [f(5) – f(3)] / 2

  1. f(5) <= f(3) + 6 => f’(y) <= 3 => True
  2. f(5) >= f(3) – 2 => f’(y) >= -1 => True
  3. f(5) <= f(3) + 10 => f’(y) <= 5 => True (If f’(y) <= 3, then f’(y) <= 5)
  4. f(5) >= f(3) – 10 => f’(y) >= -5 => True (If f’(y) >= –1, then f’(y) >= –5)

questions.qtext:
Shown below are portions of the graphs of $y=f(x), y=f^{\prime}(x)$, and $y=f^{\prime \prime}(x)$.
Determine which graph is which.
questions.solution:
Answer: B, A

Source solution 1 (score: 1)

the relationships between a function and its derivatives:

  1. $f(x)$ is the original function.
  2. $f'(x)$ represents the rate of change (slope) of $f(x)$.
  3. $f''(x)$ represents the rate of change of $f'(x)$, or the concavity of $f(x)$.

now, let's analyze the options carefully,

option A) $A = f(x), \, B = f^{\prime}(x), \, C = f^{\prime \prime}(x)$

false because when $A = f(x)$ became parellel to x-axis (slope = 0) near the intersection of $A$ and $C, \, B = f^{\prime}(x) \neq 0$.

option B) $A = f^{\prime} (x), \, B = f(x), \, C = f^{\prime \prime}(x)$

true because when $B = f(x)$ is increasing with decreasing slope then $A = f^{\prime} (x) = +ve$ and decreasing. when $B$ became parellel to X-axis then $A = 0$. when $B$ started decreasing with decreasing slope then $A$ also became more and more $-ve$ and so on $f(x)$ and $f^{\prime} (x)$ are in complete sync. similarly for $C = f^{\prime \prime} (x)$, when $A$ is decreasing then $C$ is $-ve$, when $A$ became parellel to X-axis then $C = 0$ and so on, here $A$ and $C$ are also in complete sync.

option C) $A = f^{\prime \prime}(x), \, B = f(x), \, C = f^{\prime}(x)$

false because when $B$ is increasing then also C is $-ve$, it should have been $+ve$

option D) $A = f^{\prime}(x), \, B = f^{\prime \prime}(x), \, C = f(x)$.

false because when $A = 0$ then C is not parellel to X-axis (slope = 0).

Source solution 2 (score: 0)
Answer (Option B is Correct)

The key idea is to use the relationship between a function and its derivatives:

  • If f has a local maximum/minimum, then f′(x)=0,
  • If f′(x) has a local maximum/minimum, then f′′(x)=0.
Step 1: Identify f(x)

Consider Graph B (solid curve) as f(x).

It has:

  • a local maximum (left),
  • a local minimum (middle),
  • another local maximum (right).

Therefore, its derivative must be zero at these three x-coordinates.

Now observe Graph A (dotted curve). It crosses the x-axis exactly at these turning points of Graph B.

Hence,

A=f′(x)

This is further confirmed by checking the sign of the derivative:

  • Where B is increasing, A is positive.
  • Where B is decreasing, A is negative.

Thus, the sign changes of A perfectly match the increasing/decreasing behavior of B.

Step 2: Identify f′′(x)

Since A=f′(x)), the remaining graph should be f′′(x)

Observe that Graph A has one local minimum and one local maximum.

At these points,

f′′(x)=0

Graph C (dashed curve) crosses the x-axis at these locations, confirming that

C=f′′(x)

Final Identification

A=f′(x),

B=f(x),

C=f′′(x)

Hence, the correct option is

B

questions.qtext:
Consider a continuous function $f(x),$ and suppose that $f(x)$ and its first derivative $f^{\prime}(x)$ are differentiable everywhere. Suppose we know the following information about $f(x)$ and its first and second derivatives.

  • On the interval $(-\infty,-2)$, we have $f(x)=2^{-x}$.
  • $\displaystyle\lim _{x \rightarrow \infty} f(x)=6$
  • $f(2)=-5, f(3)=7,$ and $f(4)=8$
  • $f^{\prime}(x)$ is equal to 0 at $x=-1,2,4,$ and not at any other $x$-values.
  • $f^{\prime \prime}(x)<0$ on the intervals $-1<x<0$ and $3<x<5$, and not on any other interval.

Find the global minimum of $f(x)$ on $(-\infty, \infty)?$ (minimum value of $f(x)$)
questions.solution:
Answer: 5

Source solution 1 (score: 10)

Detailed Video Solution: https://youtu.be/6aIuj2b2J38

We now must find the global minimum. We know that $f(2)=-5$ and $\displaystyle\lim _{x \rightarrow \infty} f(x)=6$, so there must be a global minimum somewhere. It can only occur at a critical point of $f(x)$, and since $f(4)=8,$ it does not occur at $x=4$. We now must decide whether the global minimum occurs at $x=2$ or $x=-1$.

Since $f^{\prime \prime}(x)<0$ on the interval $-1<x<0$, we see that $f^{\prime}(x)$ is decreasing on this interval. Since $f^{\prime}(-1)=0,$ that means that $f^{\prime}(x)$ must be negative on this interval. That means that $f(x)$ is decreasing on this interval. That means that $f(-0.5)<f(-1),$ and so the function $f(x)$ cannot have a global minimum at $x=-1$.

We conclude that the global minimum occurs at $x=2$.
